doc.title: Tim Ries interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 19, 2022

title: Mistakes, self-criticism and accepting compliments
summary: Ries says he does not think about mistakes while playing, and that only near age 50 could he accept compliments without inner criticism.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: When you’re improvising is there such a thing as a mistake for you?

Well I’m not thinking about that at the time. I’m not thinking about, because then if you get in that mindset then if you think about the mistake then you’re in that mistake, it means like — so if that takes over where you’re thinking about the mistakes rather than just the time that you’re doing this, then you inhibit not only that second that you’re in but then the upcoming thing. So I try not — of course if I listen, if I listen back to — if I recorded it, listen back I’d go uh, then you analyze and you’re your own worst critic in a

way. I try not to get in the way of that while playing because then — and it took me actually I’m now 62, it took me until I was almost 50 I think before somebody like let’s say last night. I finished the concert and many people came up and we were talking. “Oh thank you for the night, it was great, it was a lovely concert.” You know all the compliments. Now I can say, “Thank you very much. I appreciate your kind words.” And I’m able to now accept the compliment that somebody had a good time. Because up until that point until I was like 50 I would be like in my head I’m thinking, “Really? Like you enjoyed that? Because didn’t you hear those mistakes?” All of those things, that’s in our own minutiae of our own psyche. I don’t need to involve people with that. Because I don’t need to like, my own critic of myself, I don’t need to. Now I can just say I share this time with you, and like I was talking about before, you were a part of that experience too because that person changed maybe the way I play because I look out in the audience and if I’m talking a little bit before you have a connection with the — so I don’t want to ruin that experience for somebody. And so I don’t want to get in my own way, which I can, but I try my best to push aside the critique. It’s difficult.
Yeah. You don’t want to make someone regret giving you a compliment like didn’t you hear that high note I went for and I didn’t get? It’s counterproductive.

Yeah. So I try to stay away from myself and the judging. And certainly at the time of the mistake, because then you’re really trapped. Because the whole thing about improvisation, you’re trying to move forward. You’re trying to like, you don’t want to be stuck in two seconds ago, you want to be really in the now. That’s the idea, like to capture that moment right now.
